title: Cars: from go-kart to electric car
description: The forces that move and stop a car: engine, gearbox, traction, brakes, cornering, aerodynamics and batteries — up to the design of a Formula SAE car, with a vehicle dynamics simulator.

car-01-forcas.title: The forces on a car
car-01-forcas.theory:
# A car is a body under forces

Everything a car does — accelerate, brake, corner — is explained by **Newton's 2nd law**:

```
F net = m · a
```

The acceleration `a` (m/s²) is the net force `F` (newtons, N) divided by the mass `m` (kg). With the **same force**, a **lighter car accelerates more**.

## The four main forces

- **Traction force**: the engine turns the wheels and the tyre pushes the ground backwards; the ground pushes the car forwards.
- **Aerodynamic drag**: the air resists the motion. It grows with the **square** of the speed: `F_air = ½ · ρ · Cd · A · v²`.
- **Rolling resistance**: the tyre deforms as it rolls. It is roughly `Crr · m · g` (Crr ≈ 0.012 on a road tyre).
- **Weight** (`m · g`): pulls the car down and is balanced by the ground. It matters because tyre grip depends on it.

The net force is **traction − drag − rolling**. At the start drag is almost zero and the car accelerates hard; near top speed the traction barely beats the air.

## Units

- 100 km/h = 100 ÷ 3.6 = **27.8 m/s**.
- 1 kW = 1000 W; power = force × speed.

## The simulator

It integrates `F = m·a` in steps of 5 milliseconds. The engine has a realistic power curve, the gearbox shifts by itself and the tyres have a grip limit. In this lesson you only change **mass** and **power**.
car-01-forcas.task: Make the car go from **0 to 100 km/h in 8.5 s or less**. Try reducing the mass and increasing the power, and watch the speed graph.
car-01-forcas.safety: The experiments here are simulator-only. **Never** test acceleration, braking or cornering on public roads: it is a traffic offence and puts lives at risk. Real tests only on a closed track, with safety equipment and supervision.
hints: Less mass: the same force gives more acceleration (a = F/m).
More power helps, but the front tyres have a limit: try something like 1000 kg and 110 kW.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 8.5 s or less

questions.prompt: A **1000 kg** car receives a net force of **3000 N**. What is the acceleration?
Why does the car accelerate less and less as it gets faster?
options: Because the engine heats up and loses power
Because drag grows with the square of the speed and the long gears deliver less force at the wheel
Because the car's mass increases with speed
Because tyre friction disappears at high speed
questions.explanation: Drag (½·ρ·Cd·A·v²) grows a lot with speed, and in longer gears the force at the wheel is smaller. The net force shrinks, so the acceleration does too.

questions.prompt: With a constant acceleration of **4 m/s²**, how long does it take to go from 0 to 100 km/h (27.8 m/s)?

car-02-motor.title: Engine: torque, power and revs
car-02-motor.theory:
# Torque and power

The engine produces **torque** (`T`, in N·m): the "turning force" on the crankshaft. **Power** is torque times rotational speed:

```
P = T · ω        with  ω = rpm · 2π / 60   (rad/s)
```

Example: 200 N·m at 3000 rpm → ω = 314 rad/s → P = 62,800 W = **62.8 kW**.

## The engine curve

A combustion engine does not deliver the same torque at every rpm. In this simulator we use the classic approximation:

```
P(x) = Pmax · (x + x² − x³)     x = rpm / rpm at maximum power
```

This gives **maximum torque at half** the max-power rpm (1.25 · Pmax/ωpk) and a **redline** at 1.15 times that rpm. Above it the engine cuts out.

- **Torque** defines the "push" in each gear.
- **Power** defines how fast you can go: at **top speed** the engine power (minus losses, ~10%) is all spent against the air and rolling: `P = (F_air + F_roll) · v`.

## Old units

- 1 cv (metric horsepower) = 0.7355 kW; 1 hp = 0.7457 kW.
- A small family car has ~60–80 kW; a sports car, 200–400 kW.

## Play and observe

Increase the **power** and watch the top speed rise. Change the **max-power rpm**: for the same power, more rpm means **less torque**.
car-02-motor.task: Give the car a **top speed of at least 210 km/h** and **0–100 km/h in 9 s or less**.
hints: Top speed depends on power: drag requires P ∝ v³.
With about 110 kW the car exceeds 210 km/h.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 9 s or less

questions.prompt: An engine delivers **200 N·m at 3000 rpm**. What is the power, in kW?
A **120 cv** engine has how many kW? (1 cv = 0.7355 kW)
Why is it **power** (and not just torque) that defines the top speed?
options: Because torque does not reach the wheels
Because at top speed the engine power equals the power spent against the air and rolling (force × speed)
Because the gearbox turns power into mass
questions.explanation: Power = force × speed. At constant speed, all the power at the wheel goes into beating drag and rolling; the gearbox can multiply torque but does not create power.

car-03-cambio.title: Gearbox: multiplying the torque
car-03-cambio.theory:
# Why does a car have gears?

The engine only works well in a range of revs (here, up to 1.15 × the max-power rpm). The wheels, however, turn from 0 up to thousands of rpm. The **gearbox** is a set of gears that trades **speed for torque**.

```
Wheel torque = T_engine × i_gear × i_differential × efficiency
Wheel force  = Wheel torque / wheel radius
Speed        = (rpm · 2π / 60) · radius / (i_gear × i_differential)
```

- **Large ratio** (short gear, e.g. 1st = 3.5): lots of torque, little speed.
- **Small ratio** (long gear, e.g. 0.8): little torque, lots of speed.
- The **differential** multiplies all the gears (e.g. 4.0).

## Choosing the ratios

- 1st gear too short: the wheel spins or 1st runs out quickly.
- Last gear too short: the engine hits the cut-off before the air limits the car — **low top speed**.
- Few gears with big jumps: after each shift the revs drop a lot and the engine leaves its good range.

In the simulator the intermediate ratios follow a **geometric progression** between 1st and the last, and each shift takes 0.2 s without traction. The car has all-wheel drive so that the limit is the engine, not the tyre.
car-03-cambio.task: Choose the number of gears and the ratios to make **0–100 km/h in 8 s or less** without losing the **200 km/h top speed**.
hints: Increase 1st gear and the differential to accelerate harder.
More gears keep the engine near maximum power. Try 6 gears, 1st = 3.5, last = 0.8 and differential 3.6.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 8 s or less

questions.prompt: The engine delivers **150 N·m**. With 1st gear of **3.5** and differential of **4.0**, what is the wheel torque (no losses)?
With that 2100 N·m torque on a wheel of radius **0.30 m**, what is the force on the ground?
What happens if **all** the gears are too short (large ratios)?
options: The car is slower at everything
It accelerates hard, but the engine reaches the cut-off early and the top speed drops
The top speed increases a lot
questions.explanation: Large ratios multiply the torque, but make the engine spin faster for the same speed; in the last gear it hits the rev limit before drag limits the car.

car-04-tracao.title: Traction and weight transfer
car-04-tracao.theory:
# The tyre's limit

A tyre only transmits force up to a limit: **F_max = μ · N**, where μ is the friction coefficient (≈ 0.9 on dry asphalt, 1.5 on racing tyres) and N is the normal force (the weight resting on that tyre). Beyond that, the wheel **spins** — and a spinning tyre transmits **less** force (kinetic friction < static).

## Weight transfer

When the car accelerates, the weight "goes backwards"; when it brakes, it "goes forwards". The amount is:

```
ΔW = m · a · h / L
```

- `h` = height of the centre of gravity (CG), `L` = wheelbase.
- High CG or short wheelbase → more transfer.

## Which wheels pull?

- **Front (FWD)**: cheap and compact, but when accelerating the front gets **lighter** — it spins easily with a lot of power.
- **Rear (RWD)**: gains weight when accelerating; great for high power.
- **All-wheel (AWD)**: uses the weight on all four wheels: maximum acceleration ≈ μ · g.

In the simulator the driver floors it: if the engine force exceeds the tyre limit, it counts the **wheelspin** time and the tyre then transmits only 85% of the limit.
car-04-tracao.task: This car has **160 kW** and front-wheel drive: it spins a lot. Adjust the drive and the weight distribution to make **0–100 km/h in 6 s or less** and **spin for 2 s at most**.
hints: With front-wheel drive, the weight leaves the front when accelerating.
All-wheel drive uses all four wheels: try AWD.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 6 s or less

questions.prompt: A **1300 kg** car accelerating at **4 m/s²**, CG at **0.55 m** height and wheelbase of **2.6 m**. How much weight (in N) moves from the front to the rear?
Why do very powerful cars usually have **rear** or **all-wheel** drive?
options: Because the engine is closer to the wheels
Because when accelerating the weight goes backwards, increasing the grip of the rear wheels
Because the rear wheels are bigger
Because front-wheel drive uses more fuel
questions.explanation: Weight transfer increases the normal force at the rear; since F_max = μ·N, the rear wheels can take more force.

questions.prompt: With all-wheel drive and μ = 0.9, what is the greatest possible acceleration (ignoring the air)?
questions.explanation: With all the weight on the driven wheels: a = μ·g = 0.9 × 9.81 ≈ 8.83 m/s².

car-05-frenagem.title: Braking, ABS and reaction time
car-05-frenagem.theory:
# Stopping is physics too

The total stopping distance has two parts:

```
Reaction distance = v · t_reaction
Braking distance ≈ v² / (2 · a)
```

- At 100 km/h (27.8 m/s), each **1 s** of reaction is **27.8 m** before you touch the brake.
- Braking depends on **v²**: double the speed gives **four times** the distance.
- The best possible is `a = μ · g`: with μ = 0.9 → 8.8 m/s² → **44 m** from 100 km/h.

## Brake balance and lock-up

When braking, the weight goes to the **front** (ΔW = m·a·h/L). That is why the front brakes do 65–80% of the work (the **balance**). If a wheel asks for more force than μ·N, it **locks**:

- **Front** wheels locked: the car does not obey the steering wheel (it goes straight).
- **Rear** wheels locked: the rear slides and the car **spins** — very dangerous.
- A locked tyre drags with only ~75% of the friction: the distance increases.

## ABS

**ABS** (anti-lock braking system) measures the speed of each wheel and eases the brake when it starts to lock, keeping the tyre near maximum friction (in the simulator, 95% of the limit) and the car controllable.
car-05-frenagem.task: At 100 km/h, with a distracted driver (1.5 s reaction), the car stops too far away. Make the **braking at most 50 m**, the **total stop at most 80 m** and **without locking the rear wheels**.
car-05-frenagem.safety: Real braking distances depend on tyres, road surface and attention. **Never** use your phone while driving: 2 seconds looking at the screen at 100 km/h is 55 m travelled blind. Do not do braking tests on public roads.
hints: More brake force shortens the braking, but may lock the wheels. ABS prevents the lock-up.
A 1.5 s reaction costs 42 m! An attentive driver reacts in about 1 s. Try ABS on, 14 kN and 1 s reaction.

questions.prompt: At **100 km/h**, how many metres does the car travel during **1 s** of reaction?
questions.explanation: 100 km/h = 27.8 m/s; in 1 s the car travels 27.8 m without braking.

questions.prompt: At **72 km/h** (20 m/s), with μ = 0.8, what is the shortest possible braking distance?
If the speed doubles, the braking distance…
questions.explanation: The distance depends on v²: (2v)² = 4v². That is why small excesses in speed increase the distance a lot.

car-06-curvas.title: Corners, tyres and rollover
car-06-curvas.theory:
# The force that makes the turn

To go in a circle, the car needs a force towards the **centre** of the curve (centripetal force):

```
F = m · v² / r        lateral acceleration = v² / r
```

The **tyres** provide this force, up to the limit `μ · m · g`. Equating:

```
v_max = √(μ · g · r)
```

- A 50 m corner with μ = 0.9 → v_max = 21 m/s = **76 km/h**.
- Doubling μ does **not** double the speed: it grows with the **root**.
- Beyond the limit: the car **understeers** and widens its path.

Lateral acceleration is usually given in **g**: 1 g = 9.81 m/s². Road cars reach ~0.9 g; race cars, 1.5 g or more.

## Rollover

In a corner, weight also transfers to the **outside** wheels. If the lateral acceleration exceeds

```
a_rollover = g · track / (2 · h_CG)
```

the inside wheels lift and the car **rolls over before it slides**. That is why SUVs (high CG) roll over more and race cars are low and wide.

## Downforce

Wings and the car's underbody push the car **against the ground** (`½·ρ·ClA·v²`). More normal force → more grip, without more mass. But it only shows up at **high speed**.
car-06-curvas.task: The corner has a **radius of 50 m** and you must take it at **90 km/h** (at least **1.2 g** of lateral acceleration) **without leaving the track** and **without risk of rolling over**.
hints: v_max = √(μ·g·r): for 90 km/h (25 m/s) on 50 m you need μ ≥ 1.28.
Grippier tyres (μ = 1.3) solve it; if you raise μ too much, the car risks rolling over — lower the CG.
goals: Takes the corner without leaving the track

questions.prompt: What is the maximum speed in a corner of **100 m** radius with μ = **0.8**?
A utility vehicle has a track width of **1.5 m** and CG at **0.75 m**. From how many g does it tend to roll over?
questions.explanation: a/g = track / (2·h) = 1.5 / 1.5 = 1.0 g. If the tyres can take more than that, it rolls over before it slides.

questions.prompt: Why are race cars low and wide?
options: A low CG and wide track raise the rollover limit and reduce weight transfer
questions.explanation: The rollover limit is track/(2h): low and wide raises that limit and reduces the lateral weight transfer, which worsens the total grip.

car-07-aerodinamica.title: Aerodynamics and fuel consumption
car-07-aerodinamica.theory:
# The air is the biggest enemy on the road

The drag force is:

```
F_air = ½ · ρ · Cd · A · v²
```

- `ρ` ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ (air density), `A` = frontal area (m²), `Cd` = drag coefficient (the car's shape).
- Typical Cd: truck 0.6–0.8; small family car 0.33; efficient car 0.22–0.26.

The **power** to beat the air is force × speed:

```
P_air = ½ · ρ · Cd · A · v³
```

With **v³**, double the speed requires **8 times** the power. From ~60 km/h on, the air spends more than rolling.

## From the engine to the tank

- Power at the wheel = (F_air + F_rolling) · v.
- The gearbox loses ~10%; a petrol engine turns only **20–35%** of the fuel energy into work (the rest becomes heat).
- 1 litre of petrol ≈ **8.9 kWh**.

```
Consumption (L/100 km) = Energy per km / 8.9 kWh × 100
```

Reducing **Cd·A** also raises the top speed, because there is power left over.
car-07-aerodinamica.task: On the highway, at **120 km/h**, make the car use **at most 7 L/100 km** and reach **205 km/h** top speed — by improving the aerodynamics.
hints: Drag depends on Cd × A. Reduce both.
A car with Cd 0.26 and an area of 1.9 m² reaches both goals.

questions.prompt: What is the drag force on a car with Cd = **0.30**, A = **2.2 m²**, at **30 m/s** (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³)?
What power (in kW) is spent just against that drag at 30 m/s?
If the speed doubles, the power spent against the air…
questions.explanation: The force grows with v² and the power with v³: 2³ = 8.

car-08-suspensao.title: Suspension: springs, dampers and handling
car-08-suspensao.theory:
# What is the suspension for?

The suspension keeps the **tyres on the ground** (grip) and the **car stable and comfortable**. The two basic elements:

- **Spring**: stores energy and supports the weight. Force = `k · x` (k = stiffness, N/m; x = deflection).
- **Damper**: turns the motion into heat and **stops the oscillation**. Without it the car would keep bouncing like a ball.

## The "quarter car" model

Each wheel supports ~1/4 of the mass. Spring + mass form an oscillator with natural frequency:

```
f = (1 / 2π) · √(k / m)
```

- Passenger cars: **1.0–1.5 Hz** (soft, comfortable).
- Race cars: **2–5 Hz** (hard, little roll).

The static deflection (how much the spring sinks when stationary) is `x = m·g / k`.

## Behaviour in corners

- **Understeer** (front slides out): the front loses grip first; the car takes a wider turn than the steering asks for.
- **Oversteer** (rear slides out): the rear slides; the car turns more than requested.
- **Anti-roll bar**: links the wheels of the same axle and reduces the body **roll**; stiffening the front bar increases understeer.
- **Camber**: the wheel's tilt seen from the front. A little negative camber keeps the tyre better planted in the corner.

## Common geometries

- **MacPherson**: simple and cheap (most small cars).
- **Double wishbone**: controls camber better; used in sports cars and Formula SAE.
- **Torsion beam**: rear of compact cars.

questions.prompt: A quarter car has **300 kg** and a spring of **30,000 N/m**. What is the natural frequency?
What is the main function of the **damper**?
options: Support the weight of the car
Dissipate energy and make the spring's oscillation stop quickly
questions.explanation: The spring supports the weight; the damper turns the motion energy into heat, preventing the car from continuing to oscillate.

questions.prompt: In a corner, the car widens its path even with the steering wheel turned: the front wheels lost grip first. This is…
questions.explanation: Understeer (front slides out) is when the front axle reaches its limit before the rear.

questions.prompt: With the same spring (30,000 N/m) and 300 kg, how much does the spring sink when stationary?
What does the **anti-roll bar** do?
options: Absorbs bumps on one wheel only
questions.explanation: It twists when one side goes up and the other down, resisting roll; that is why it keeps the car "flatter" in corners.

car-09-eletrico.title: Electric car: energy and range
car-09-eletrico.theory:
# Electric: fewer parts, different physics

An electric motor delivers **maximum torque from 0 rpm** and keeps **constant power** at high revs. That is why the electric car uses **a single gear** (a reduction of ~9:1) and pulls away very strongly.

```
Wheel force = min( T_motor · reduction / radius ,  P_motor / v ) × 0.95
```

## Energy and range

- Battery: capacity in **kWh** (energy). An average car has 40–80 kWh.
- Typical consumption: **13–20 kWh/100 km**.
- Battery-to-wheel efficiency is high: **85–92%** (petrol: 20–35%).

```
Range (km) = Capacity (kWh) / Consumption (kWh/100 km) × 100
```

## The weight dilemma

Batteries are heavy: current packs store ~**160 Wh/kg**. A 75 kWh battery weighs ~470 kg! More battery = more range, but also more mass (worse acceleration and more rolling resistance). The simulator adds the battery mass to the car.

## Regenerative braking

When braking, the motor becomes a **generator** and returns part of the energy to the battery — which is why electric cars use little in city traffic (the simulator only measures the highway at constant speed, without regeneration).
car-09-eletrico.task: Design an electric car with a **range of at least 400 km at 100 km/h** that does **0–100 km/h in 7 s or less**.
car-09-eletrico.safety: Electric car batteries work at **400 to 800 V** direct current: lethal voltage. Only trained technicians with insulated equipment work on the high-voltage system (orange cables). Damaged lithium batteries can catch fire hours later; never puncture or heat cells.
hints: A bigger battery gives range, but is heavy: compensate with efficiency and aerodynamics.
Try 75 kWh, 90% efficiency, a 150 kW and 350 N·m motor with all-wheel drive.
goals: 0 to 100 km/h in 7 s or less

questions.prompt: A car with a **60 kWh** battery uses **15 kWh/100 km**. What is the range?
How much does a **60 kWh** pack weigh at **160 Wh/kg**?
Why do electric cars usually use **less** in the city than on the highway (the opposite of petrol cars)?
options: Because in the city the speed is low (little drag) and regenerative braking recovers energy
Because the electric motor has an automatic gearbox
Because city air is less dense
questions.explanation: Drag grows with v², and when braking the motor works as a generator and recharges the battery.

car-10-projeto-fsae.title: Project: lap time of a Formula SAE car
car-10-projeto-fsae.theory:
# Engineering is compromise

In **Formula SAE**, university teams design and build a small race car (~300 kg with driver, ~60 kW with an intake restrictor). What matters is the **lap time**, and almost every decision improves one thing and worsens another.

## The lap model

Our track is an oval: two 75 m straights and two 180° corners with a 15 m radius. The simulator does what a track engineer does in a spreadsheet ("point-mass simulation"):

- **Corners** at the tyre limit: `v = √(μ·g·r)`, or, with downforce,

```
m·v²/r = μ·(m·g + ½·ρ·ClA·v²)   →   v² = μ·m·g / (m/r − μ·ρ·ClA/2)
```

- **Straights**: maximum acceleration (engine, gears and traction) from the corner exit speed, and braking at the limit (`μ·(m·g + downforce)`) to reach the next corner at the right speed.
- Time = sum of distance / speed in each section.

## The design levers

- **Downforce (ClA)**: faster corners, shorter braking — but the wing has drag (here ClA/3), which **steals speed on the straight**.
- **Mass**: less mass helps everything (corner, straight and braking), but the rules and safety impose a minimum.
- **Gear ratios**: on a tight layout, shorter gears keep the engine in its power band.

On tracks with long straights, the optimum is **less wing**; on tight tracks (like FSAE), **more wing** usually wins. Test both limits and watch the speed graph along the lap.
car-10-projeto-fsae.task: Do a lap in **12.5 s at most** while keeping at least **100 km/h at the end of the straight** (the car must not become a "brick" with too much wing).
hints: Add downforce little by little and watch the lap time and the top speed on the straight.
Combine ClA ≈ 4, differential 4.5 and a mass of 280 kg.
goals: Speed at the end of the straight ≥ 100 km/h

questions.prompt: With no downforce, μ = **1.4** and a radius of **15 m**, what is the maximum corner speed?
With m = **300 kg**, μ = **1.5**, r = **15 m**, ρ = 1.2 kg/m³ and ClA = **3 m²**, what is the maximum corner speed?
On a track with **very long straights** and few corners, what tends to give the best time?
options: Little wing: drag costs more on the straights than the extra grip gains in the corners
questions.explanation: The wing's gain shows up in the corners; the cost (drag) shows up on every straight. With long straights, the cost dominates (in the same model, with 250 m straights, the best ClA drops to about 1).
